title: SMSF debt ban underestimated non-bank loans
full_text:
Non-bank lenders wrote more than 16,000 residential loans to self-managed superannuation funds last year, more than four times the total the federal government cited when justifying a ban on SMSFs borrowing to buy homes, new Australian Finance Industry Association figures show.
The industry body said its 150 members wrote the loans in the 12 months to June and that data the federal government cited last month of just 4000 loans to SMSF borrowers vastly underestimated the total.
As a result of that underestimation, Labor's ban on residential borrowing by SMSFs could have an even greater impact on the market than expected, especially for investment in new housing, according to the AFIA.
"This is not a small or marginal segment of the lending market," said AFIA chief executive Diane Tate, who will argue the point at a Senate estimates hearing on Monday. "Our members alone wrote over 16,000 new residential SMSF loans in FY26. The ATO estimate of 4000 per year is based on data that Treasury officials have acknowledged is about three years old. The policy was designed around an incomplete picture and supposedly a review conducted well over a decade ago."
AFIA said its members account for more than three-quarters of the specialist non-bank lender market.
The industry body did not give a breakdown in its figures between lending for established housing and lending to build new homes, saying not all of its members recorded the split.
But the purchase of brand-new homes "dominates" the volume of lending to SMSFs, said Ashley Bramich, commercial agency Colliers' director of project marketing, adding that the new policy, due to come into effect on August 10, had triggered an "avalanche" of demand from SMSF borrowers wanting to beat the deadline, according to wealth advisers, accountants and other people in the off-the-plan sales industry.
This would lead to stalled developments after that date, he said.
"The numbers will be about 2000 sales throughout Australia from when legislation passed to its implementation on August 10, based on what we are transacting and seeing," Bramich said. "The big concern, however, is that the development industry for affordable projects could fall off the cliff after August 10, as this cohort of buyers will disappear and not be replaced."
In announcing the measure, which it accepted to secure the Greens' support for the budget restriction on negative gearing and use of the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount for investors, the government argued that banning SMSFs from borrowing to buy housing would further reduce the competition for first-home buyers.
But the housing industry argued the move is an own-goal for a federal government pushing what it already calls an ambitious - and unlikely to be realised - goal of building 1.2 million new homes in five years to ease Australia's chronic housing shortage.
Even if the number of SMSF loans for new builds was only 4000, the concentration of them at the early stage of development meant they played a significant role in providing developers with the early presales that they needed to justify construction funding with lenders and market a project more widely to other buyers.
A rough estimate of two to three homes for every SMSF purchase meant that stopping 4000 loans could mean up to 12,000 homes did not get built, the Urban Development Institute of Australia said earlier this month.
"SMSF purchases play a critical role in securing the pre-sales required to finance and unlock new housing projects," said UDIA national president Oscar Stanley. "Remove those buyers and we will see projects delayed or shelved altogether. Policy levers should be used to enhance housing supply, not to reduce or delay it."
AFIA's Tate said an exemption should be granted under the existing ban on residential lending to SMSFs to permit them to keep investing in new builds.
"The government has already drawn a principled distinction between new and established residential dwellings in its capital gains tax and negative gearing reforms, preserving full concessions for new dwellings to encourage housing supply," she said. "Applying that same logic to SMSF borrowing is internally consistent, uses the government's own drafting, and does not reopen the core policy agreement."
